storyboard.claim: The past is recruited to serve a purpose chosen right now; the shut-in refuses to leave by choice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The shut-in's closed bedroom door beside the philosopher, who points back at the present as he explains the choice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Picks up the teleology thread from the broken-gear metaphor: purpose now, not cause then.
storyboard.addedInformation: The door makes 'the friend locked in his room' literal and plants the choice in the present moment.

storyboard.claim: Anxiety is manufactured as a means to reach the prior goal of not going out.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A target beside the uneasy young man: the goal was aimed at before the anxiety appeared.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the goal that the closed door of the previous beat was serving.
storyboard.addedInformation: The target shows the goal as chosen and aimed at rather than something that happened to him.

storyboard.claim: The young man objects: calling crippling panic a self-run strategy sounds incredibly dismissive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man holds up a hand to stop the philosopher, mid-objection, eyebrows raised.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pushes back against the goal-first reading the last two beats established.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: no icon — a mask here would wrongly imply panic really is faked; the raised hand carries the objection.

storyboard.claim: Adler is not saying the physical symptoms are faked — the palpitations and shaking are very real.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The phrase 'symptoms are faked' struck through while the philosopher denies it with an open, steady hand.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the young man's faking question with a direct rejection.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike shows the rejection without sound and keeps the beat from reading as an accusation.

storyboard.claim: The symptoms are deeply felt; what Adler challenges is only the direction of causality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher turns his pointing finger from the past side back toward the present side.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From what is real (the symptoms) to what is being reframed (their direction).
storyboard.addedInformation: The turned finger makes 'direction' physical: the dispute is about arrow order, not denial.

storyboard.claim: The philosopher's clarifying analogy opens: a terrible cold with a dangerously high fever.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher plays the doctor, examining the young man with a magnifier.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Begins the illustration the previous beat promised.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns the hypothetical example into a visible doctor's visit so the analogy has actors.

storyboard.claim: The doctor explains today's fever by yesterday's freezing rain without a jacket.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A rainstorm cloud over the young man, coatless — the past event the doctor blames.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Supplies the past cause for the fever established in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Keeps the cause visibly in the past weather while the patient stays in the present frame.

storyboard.claim: The explanation may be factually true, but the doctor stops there and only pats your shoulder.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher gives the young man a consoling shoulder pat and offers nothing else.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the doctor's true explanation into the actual problem: he quits before treating.
storyboard.addedInformation: The useless pat shows the dead end of causal explanation far better than the sentence alone.

storyboard.claim: A patient hearing only yesterday's story for today's fever would be furious.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man flares up, hand thrust out, demanding treatment instead of a history lesson.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reacts to the shoulder pat of the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the correct response visible: anger at a true-but-useless explanation, not gratitude.

storyboard.claim: Staring at yesterday's cause never cures today's suffering; the symptom has to be treated now.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A clock above the feverish young man: the fever is happening in this hour, not in the rain.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States what the furious patient demands in place of the doctor's story.
storyboard.addedInformation: The clock pins the argument on the present moment where treatment can actually happen.

storyboard.claim: Etiology explains why you got sick and offers no medicine; teleology asks what you are doing with the illness now.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-step chain: the causal explanation leads straight to an empty treatment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Condenses the doctor analogy into the etiology-versus-teleology distinction it was built to prove.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the dead end of past-cause thinking as an arrow instead of a paragraph.

storyboard.claim: Dwelling on past causes is treating your own life like a true crime podcast.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man holding a case file of notes, reading his own life as evidence.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the etiology habit from the diagram in the hosts' own modern analogy.
storyboard.addedInformation: The case notes make the analogy physical: he is hunting a culprit rather than healing.

storyboard.claim: We obsessively hunt for the killer in our past: the bad teacher, the absent parent.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man searching his memory, brow furrowed, running through the suspects of his upbringing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lists the suspects inside the true-crime analogy just introduced.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: no icon — a magnifier or photo would read as real detective work; the searching face carries it.

storyboard.claim: Finding the killer does not resurrect the victim and does not fix the present.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher waves off the hunt with an open hand: the present is untouched either way.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Cuts off the killer hunt of the previous beat as useless to now.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: no icon — a grave would read as a real death rather than the podcast metaphor.

storyboard.claim: The shut-in's fear is real, and its purpose is to keep him safely inside.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A shield hovering at the closed door as the philosopher points out the fear's job.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns from the podcast analogy to the shut-in's actual fear.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shield shows fear acting as protection, which is the teleological move being made.

storyboard.claim: Declaring 'I am a victim of my past' buys a permanent, socially acceptable hall pass.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man holding a mask at arm's length in front of his own face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the payoff of the protective fear from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask shows the victim identity as something worn for an audience, not a fact about him.

storyboard.claim: Fear functions as the bodyguard of the goal of avoiding failure — it comes first.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-step chain: the fear stands first as the bodyguard, and avoiding failure is what it protects.
storyboard.onScreenText: the fear -> the bodyguard -> avoiding failure
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the mechanism behind the hall pass described in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the order explicit: fear guards a goal, so fear is a tool rather than a cause.

storyboard.claim: The strategy comes first and the excuse of the past follows to justify it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man slumped under a trailing excuse — 'my trauma made me this way' hanging behind him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The excuse is the second half of the chain the diagram just laid out.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the excuse trailing the choice instead of producing it, which is the whole reversal.

callout.text: whose task is it to change today

storyboard.claim: Blaming the past refuses the hard question: whose task is it to change today?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher aims the question at the young man, who looks away from it.
storyboard.onScreenText: whose task is it to change today
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the excuse just named into the question that excuse exists to avoid.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the book's central question on screen as something aimed at the person making excuses.

storyboard.claim: Dropping the untouchable past-excuse is a harsh pill, which is why Adler's approach is called a psychology of courage.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher stands squarely and delivers the hard line without flinching.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the price of the question from the previous beat: courage.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: no icon — no symbol reads 'courage' literally; the steady posture carries it.

storyboard.claim: No experience causes success or failure by itself; we give each experience the meaning that suits us.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher sets one event down and re-reads it, weighing a second meaning for it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Supplies the principle underneath the courage the previous beat demanded.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows meaning as something a person assigns to an event rather than something found inside it.

storyboard.claim: With the past-excuse gone there is nowhere to hide: we must face our current flaws.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man holds a mirror and studies his own face, nowhere to look away.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The consequence of assigning meaning ourselves: only self-examination is left.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mirror makes 'look at your flaws' literal and keeps the gaze on himself, not on his past.

storyboard.claim: The scene resets: the youth begins explaining to the philosopher why he feels so terrible about himself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Both men back in the study, the youth leaning forward to open his account of himself.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the general argument to the youth's personal case.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the transition into the book's next pillar: feelings of inferiority.

storyboard.claim: In a cafe he reads about a man his exact same age who is wildly successful, wealthy and thriving.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth alone at a cafe table, reading a newspaper article about a man his exact same age.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The specific scene that produces the feeling the youth is trying to explain.
storyboard.addedInformation: The age match is the engine of comparison: the man in the article is the same age, not a superior generation.

storyboard.claim: Reading it, he feels a hot flush of envy and touches his own pimpled face, drowning in lacks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth at the table reaching up to his own face, ashamed of what he sees.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the successful stranger to the youth's bodily self-comparison.
storyboard.addedInformation: The hand on the face turns envy into visible physical shame, exactly as the narration describes.

storyboard.claim: He feels he is drowning in objective worthlessness.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Water rising around the seated youth as he tells the philosopher he is drowning.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the feeling that the flush of envy produced at the cafe.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the drowning metaphor visible so the claim survives the mute test.

storyboard.claim: He insists this is no teleological excuse: he is factually, undeniably inferior to that man.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth points at the gap between himself on a low rung and the man above him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Converts the drowning feeling from the last beat into a claim of objective fact.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ladder makes the comparison vertical — someone stands above him, which is precisely his point.

storyboard.claim: Feelings of inferiority are universal, and Alfred Adler himself coined the term in this context.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler introduced on screen, book in hand, holding the term he gave psychology.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings on the authority who will answer the youth's claim of objective fact.
storyboard.addedInformation: Putting Adler himself on screen signals the shift to his own doctrine.

storyboard.claim: Adler's crucial distinction: feelings of inferiority are subjective interpretations, not objective facts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher holds two hands apart — interpretation on one side, objective fact on the other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly answers the youth's 'factually inferior' claim from two beats earlier.
storyboard.addedInformation: The physical split shows this is a difference between two kinds of statement, not two feelings.

storyboard.claim: He objects: low money, short stature and lacking a college degree look like plain objective facts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth ticks off his list of indisputable facts, a school building behind the degree he names.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Challenges the interpretation-versus-fact distinction with concrete everyday examples.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names one of the three examples on screen so the objection stays specific rather than abstract.

storyboard.claim: The book answers with the wellwater analogy: deep groundwater stays at a constant 60° all year.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher asks about deep well water and names the temperature that never moves.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the analogy that will defuse the youth's list of supposed facts.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the objective fact that the drawn cup of water in the next beats will orbit.

storyboard.claim: The objective fact is that the water is precisely 60° and does not change.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher states the fixed measurement flatly, no gesture, nothing to argue with.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Establishes the invariant half of the analogy before the feeling half arrives.
storyboard.addedInformation: Separates the fact that never changes from the feelings that are about to swing.

storyboard.claim: The same 60° water feels refreshingly cool when you drink it in the blazing summer heat.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth outdoors on a hot afternoon, drinking from the cup and visibly refreshed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the unchanging 60° fact to the first of two contrasting conditions.
storyboard.addedInformation: Fire for the heat plus a refreshed face shows fact unchanged, feeling changed.

storyboard.claim: In freezing winter the same water feels warm — only the subjective lens and context changed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Split frame: the identical cup and the same youth, summer light on one side, winter on the other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the analogy with the opposite feeling from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The split holds the invariant object and the changing environment in one glance.

storyboard.claim: The inferiority you attach to your degree or your looks is just the summer-or-winter lens you choose, depending on who you compare yourself to.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth turning the comparison over in his mind, a mirror marking how he reads himself.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transfers the wellwater analogy from water onto the youth's own facts.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mirror shows the lens is aimed at the self, and comparison is what points it.

storyboard.claim: A curated feed of fitness models and billionaires is what makes an ordinary life read as inferior.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth on his bed scrolling his phone, the objective fact being only him sitting in his room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the comparison lens a concrete modern mechanism.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phone turns the lens into an everyday object every viewer recognizes instantly.

storyboard.claim: The algorithm did not create his reality; it only supplied the lens he judges himself through.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher gestures between the phone and the unchanged room: the world itself is untouched.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Limits the power of the mechanism introduced in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Draws the line between world and lens that the narration asserts but never pictures.

storyboard.claim: Adler says a simple feeling of inferiority is actually a healthy thing, not a disease.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler presents the positive reading of the feeling, calm and unhurried.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reverses the verdict: the feeling that read as drowning can be healthy.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: no icon — no symbol reads 'healthy lack' literally; Adler's presence carries the authority.

storyboard.claim: The feeling is a launchpad: sensing you lack, you strive to improve — like the chef refining his craft.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth reaching up the next rung, effort replacing the slump of the earlier scenes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the healthy version of the feeling works instead of trapping him.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns the metaphor into an action — climbing rather than drowning.

storyboard.claim: The danger comes when that feeling rots and hardens into an inferiority complex.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth slumped beneath a heavy boulder where the light launchpad feeling used to be.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the launchpad of the previous beat into its failure mode.
storyboard.addedInformation: The boulder shows hardening and weight: now the complex carries him instead of him using it.
